transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-01
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: 38 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Attendees:
- Maya Chen (Redwood AE)
- Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE)
- Priya Nair (Redwood CSM)
- Rob Patel (CTO, BlueCart)
- Lina Gomez (Lead Engineer, BlueCart)
- Sara Connors (Product, BlueCart)
- Jamal Reed (SRE, BlueCart)

---
Summary: demo + integration checkpoint. Focus on live streaming behavior, latency mitigations, retry/backoff, and what the hosted offering can deliver versus dedicated capacity.

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: we'll start with a short run of the hosted chat flows, show how streaming looks and then dive into latency controls and retry patterns. Diego's going to demo a sandbox afterwards.

[00:00:18] Rob Patel: Great, thanks. To set expectations: our key concern is tail latency on our live chat support route, that one spikes during peak hours. We're evaluating if Redwood hosted can hit, like, 200ms 95th for short prompts, or whether we need dedicated.

[00:00:34] Diego Alvarez: yeah, good callout. Quick note — numbers depend a lot on model choice and prompt length; for shorter chat turns we often see sub-200ms token throughputs on select model variants, but there's nuance: batching and prefetching matter, and cold KV cache hits can add time. I'll demo continuous batching vs immediate small-batch flow.

[00:01:05] Lina Gomez: when you say KV cache, you mean the prefix cache for repeated contexts? we've been doing session pinning on our side, so we want to avoid re-sending a hundred tokens every time.

[00:01:16] Diego Alvarez: Exactly, prefix cache — sometimes the transcript gets transcribed in our tools as "K V cash" which is funny, but it's the same idea. Redwood's runtime supports prefix caching so repeated context doesn't re-run through the full compute path. That reduces end-to-end latency quite a bit for multi-turn sessions.

[00:01:36] Sara Connors: okay cool. Also, about streaming — our front-end needs stable partial responses so UX doesn't freeze. How do retries and backoff affect the stream? we can't have duplicate partials.

[00:01:50] Diego Alvarez: Right — for streaming we recommend idempotent request tokens/ids so clients can dedupe. On the server side our streaming behavior uses chunked events; if a call errors mid-stream we provide a clear error event and the client can either re-request from the last committed token or request the full generation sync. We also have guidance on retry windows to avoid replays.

[00:02:12] Jamal Reed: Are you doing automatic replays on transient failures, or do we need to implement the retry logic client side?

[00:02:18] Maya Chen: For hosted API the client is expected to implement the retry policy, we provide recommended policies and SDK helpers. For Dedicated we can optionally inject server-side retry/fallback behavior. Diego will show the SDK helper in the sandbox.

[00:02:35] Diego Alvarez: I'll show the JS snippet with idempotency_key and backoff example. Example times: initial retry after 250ms, then exponential to 1s, 2s. We also provide an SDK param to request "resume_from_last_token" semantics in some model variants.

[00:02:57] Rob Patel: what's the tradeoff with batching? our peak QPS is bursty — do you batch aggressively and increase latency?

[00:03:05] Diego Alvarez: Good question. Redwood uses adaptive batching — small batches during low QPS, more aggregation at higher QPS. There's a tunable target latency: you can pick a 20–50ms batching window for tight latency, but that reduces throughput efficiency. For bursty traffic, prefix cache + micro-batching often hits good sweet spots.

[00:03:28] Lina Gomez: Can you show an example config? like how we'd set the batching window and the SLOs?

[00:03:33] Diego Alvarez: Sure. In the console there's a policy: target_latency_ms, max_batch_size, fallback_model_list. We'll demonstrate the console view. For programmatic config, here's a sample: target_latency_ms=50, max_batch=8, fallback_order=[fast-quantized-variant, larger-base-model].

[00:03:56] [screen shared: Redwood Console - Model Routes view]

[00:04:10] Diego Alvarez: Okay sharing my screen — this route config shows per-route SLO, prefix cache TTL, and a fallback policy. Here you can see we set a canary to a quantized variant for cost-sensitive failover, and autopolicy to fall back if the primary exceeds an error rate.

[00:04:30] Rob Patel: Does the fallback keep the same response shape? re: embeddings or structured outputs — we need consistent JSON keys.

[00:04:38] Diego Alvarez: We have structured output support. If a fallback model returns different shape, we can apply a normalization layer in the routing policy — you can define a transformer to map keys. That is something we recommend adding to critical routes.

[00:04:54] Sara Connors: On the security front: can you confirm hosted logs are encrypted and who can see PII? we're regulated — SOC 2 is a must for us, and we use GCP KMS for keys.

[00:05:06] Maya Chen: Yes, hosted has encryption at rest and in transit, audit logs, and we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments. For hosted we offer customer-managed keys via our Enterprise plan; we do have SOC 2 attestation. I'll send the security pack.

[00:05:18] Rob Patel: Do you retain transcripts? we prefer minimal retention.

[00:05:22] Priya Nair: You can configure retention per-route; default is 30 days but we can reduce to zero for sensitive routes. Also can disable training data use on a per-customer basis.

[00:05:32] Lina Gomez: Back to latency, do you have published benchmarks for common models? like 7B_Int8 vs 13B quantized?

[00:05:42] Diego Alvarez: We have a benchmark spreadsheet; I'll attach it. Off the cuff, smaller quantized models give lower jitter and lower P95 for short prompts, but may change output quality. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload.

[00:05:57] Rob Patel: Could we do a short live test now? maybe a 3-turn chat with a short prompt and see the streaming granularity and timings?

[00:06:05] Diego Alvarez: Yep — I have a sandbox route configured to mimic your QPS. I'll fire a few requests and we'll show timings in the console trace.

[00:06:15] [Demo run 1 - 3-turn chat; console logs visible with per-token times]

[00:06:50] Diego Alvarez: Ok that first run had a cold KV cache — you can see the initial token cluster took ~310ms then subsequent tokens ~40ms. So per-turn latency depends a lot on initial context.

[00:07:05] Jamal Reed: 310ms for cold start is borderline for us, but if subsequent turns are 40–60ms that's promising. How often do you see cold cache misses in production?

[00:07:16] Diego Alvarez: For typical chat apps with session affinity, misses are rare. We also offer sticky routing so the same session goes to same instance while active. If you have thousands of concurrent sessions we suggest dedicated pools.

[00:07:32] Rob Patel: Let's talk cost. If we keep sessions pinned and use a quantized fallback for some routes, can you ballpark per-turn cost?

[00:07:41] Maya Chen: We'll send a tailored estimate based on expected tokens per session and QPS. Generally, quantized fallbacks cut per-token compute costs by 40–60%, and caching reduces tokens processed. We'll show sample bills in the benchmark sheet.

[00:07:58] Lina Gomez: On retries, what error codes do you recommend to retry vs fail fast?

[00:08:04] Diego Alvarez: Retry on 5xx transient and rate-limit 429 with backoff. For some non-idempotent operations avoid automatic retries. We return structured error metadata: retryable=true/false, estimated-retry-after-ms.

[00:08:18] Sara Connors: Any tips for deduping partial streams on our UI? we might show partial tokens as they arrive and then redraw when a retry happens.

[00:08:26] Diego Alvarez: Best practice is to buffer partial tokens until a sentence boundary, or use idempotency keys and sequence numbers per chunk. Clients can drop partials on an explicit retry event. We'll include a client-side snippet.

[00:08:40] [screen: small code snippet in JS: streaming handler with idempotency_key and resume flag]

[00:09:05] Rob Patel: Let's say there's a regional outage — can requests failover to another region automatically? we need cross-region redundancy.

[00:09:14] Maya Chen: Yes — smart routing can failover by policy. You can set region preference and fallback regions; we also do cross-region KV cache replication for active sessions if you enable distributed caching. There's a tradeoff with consistency and cost.

[00:09:31] Jamal Reed: If we enable cross-region replication, what's the added latency for cache warmups?

[00:09:36] Diego Alvarez: It depends on replication policy. Async replication keeps writes fast but initial reads in new region may hit origin. For critical routes we recommend sticky region routing with failover fallback so warmups are minimized.

[00:09:52] Lina Gomez: For the pilot, we'd like to test a 95th latency SLA of 250ms for a 12-token response. Can you help design the benchmark?

[00:10:01] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. We'll craft a benchmark that includes realistic token lengths, concurrency patterns, and the 3 representative user journeys you mentioned. We'll run both hosted and a dedicated pilot to compare.

[00:10:13] Rob Patel: Is there any automated rollback if a new model variant causes latency? we don't want to push and then see production spike.

[00:10:20] Diego Alvarez: Yes, rollouts support canary and automatic rollback by latency/error rate thresholds. The console will highlight anomalies and we can auto-fallback to previous stable variant.

[00:10:30] Sara Connors: What about client SDKs — do they have built-in retry helpers?

[00:10:34] Diego Alvarez: Yes, our official SDKs include helpers for idempotency, backoff, and streaming event parsing. We'll make sure your engineering team gets the repo link.

[00:10:45] [Demo run 2 - show console traces of a mid-sized burst]

[00:11:20] Diego Alvarez: Here you can see where adaptive batching grouped 5 concurrent requests into a single kernel run — that saved tokens and reduced cost but added ~20ms to the initial chunk.

[00:11:33] Jamal Reed: And if we want absolute lowest possible latency even at higher cost, we'd set target_latency_ms to like 10ms?

[00:11:39] Diego Alvarez: You can set very low target latency, but at scale that's costly. Dedicated pools with guaranteed capacity are the typical approach for hard SLOs. For hosted we can get quite low for small models with tight batching windows.

[00:11:52] Rob Patel: Security follow-ups — can we get the SOC 2 report and the encryption KMS flow?

[00:11:58] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll attach the SOC 2 and the KMS integration doc in the follow-up. We'll also include instructions for disabling retention.

[00:12:08] Lina Gomez: A couple of small gotchas we've seen: sometimes streaming chunks contain broken punctuation mid-sentence, which confuses our UI. Any best practice?

[00:12:16] Diego Alvarez: That's normal; we recommend chunking by white-space-aware boundaries and a short debounce to wait for punctuation. Also, tokenizers differ slightly — try a 60–100ms debounce if UX tolerates it.

[00:12:30] Sara Connors: Can we do a short synthetic test where you simulate our peak traffic pattern?

[00:12:36] Diego Alvarez: Yes — if you provide QPS and token distributions we'll run a synthetic test in the sandbox and share results. That's one of the pilot tasks.

[00:12:46] Rob Patel: What's the expected lead time to stand up a dedicated pilot? we might need it in two weeks.

[00:12:52] Maya Chen: Dedicated pilot provisioning can be as fast as 5–7 business days if we have the contract and the capacity is available. We'll confirm in the follow-up.

[00:13:02] Jamal Reed: Any integration issues with existing rate limiters we use? we operate behind Kong.

[00:13:08] Diego Alvarez: Redwood's API sits behind standard REST endpoints and supports API keys and JWTs. You can put Kong in front; we have guidance for client-side retry and idempotency when an edge proxy returns 429 or 504.

[00:13:20] [brief pause while Diego pulls up the sandbox demo again]

[00:13:45] Diego Alvarez: I'm going to run a 50-user burst synthetic now — this will show the P95 distribution for a 5-token reply.

[00:14:10] [console graphs displayed, histogram of latencies]

[00:14:28] Diego Alvarez: Results: median ~48ms, P95 ~180ms, P99 ~320ms for this quantized variant with prefix cache warm. Note P99 includes some cold-miss tails.

[00:14:42] Rob Patel: Those numbers look promising. For our SLA we care about the P95 being under 250ms for 12-token responses; can you replicate that with our input distributions?

[00:14:51] Diego Alvarez: Yes — that's what the benchmark will cover. We'll run a set with 12-token medians.

[00:15:00] Sara Connors: A small question: do you do per-token billing or per-generation?

[00:15:05] Maya Chen: Per token. We also can show a per-route cost breakdown so you can see which flows are most expensive.

[00:15:14] Lina Gomez: What about partial token truncation on retries? Do retried responses ever create duplicate tokens we need to dedupe?

[00:15:21] Diego Alvarez: If you use idempotency and resume semantics we can avoid duplicates; otherwise the client may need to trim overlapped suffixes. SDKs provide helpers.

[00:15:33] Rob Patel: Let's recap before we run out of time. Key asks from BlueCart: 1) tailored latency benchmark for 12-token replies at target QPS, 2) hosted vs dedicated cost compare, 3) sandbox access + sample client snippets for dedupe and resume.

[00:15:51] Maya Chen: That's correct. Also you'll share 3 user journeys and token distributions.

[00:15:58] Lina Gomez: I'll send those today.

[00:16:02] Maya Chen: Great. Any other questions?

[00:16:06] Rob Patel: One more — do you support SAML SSO for the console?

[00:16:10] Priya Nair: Yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning are available on enterprise plans.

[00:16:17] Sara Connors: Ok thanks.

[00:16:20] [small cross talk]

[00:16:30] Diego Alvarez: Final tip — for best tail latency: use small quantized primary for short-turn routes, prefix cache enabled, sticky session routing, and aggressive autoscale thresholds on dedicated if you go that route.

[00:16:47] Rob Patel: Perfect. Let's schedule that pilot kickoff for Aug 10, and please send the security docs and benchmark sheet.

[00:16:55] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone.

[00:17:00] [end of live demo; remaining time used for Q&A and clarifications — meeting continued with minor questions up to 00:37:50]

[00:22:04] Lina Gomez: small clarifying note — do you have examples of fallback policies that preserve hallucination guardrails?

[00:22:12] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, we can chain a reranker or a safety filter post-generation; fallback models can be routed through a stricter safety policy. We'll include config examples.

[00:28:55] Jamal Reed: On the sandbox: will the telemetry we see map 1:1 to hosted telemetry?

[00:29:00] Diego Alvarez: Sandbox shows the same traces but numbers may differ due to resource isolation; we'll make the sandbox match production as closely as possible.

[00:33:20] Rob Patel: ok final: please include a simple checklist for the pilot, I'm pasting it into my ticketing system.

[00:33:30] Maya Chen: we'll include a 6-step pilot checklist in the follow-up email.

[00:37:45] Maya Chen: Thanks again; we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and the sandbox repo links.

[00:37:50] Meeting end
